title: China’s snooping around Pacific undersea cables raises risks for Big Tech
gist: A US-China Commission report ranks trans-Pacific subsea cables by gray-zone sabotage risk, with Google, Meta and Verizon-linked cables in the top five, while CSIS finds Chinese research ships unusually active near cables; Russia and Iran pose parallel threats.

insights.claim: A US-China Economic and Security Review Commission report built a Trans-Pacific Cable Gray Zone Vulnerability Index scoring cables by depth, shipping traffic, ownership, Chinese territorial claims and Taiwan connection.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
entities: US-China Economic and Security Review Commission
insights.so_what: The index can steer where sensors and patrols go; watch which cables get protection funding.

insights.claim: Risk is highest around Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines because cables to the US pass through shallow, busy shipping lanes.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Asia-US data routes concentrate risk geographically.

insights.claim: Google's TPU, Meta's ORCA and the Verizon-co-owned E2A cables all scored in the top five most at-risk trans-Pacific cables, and several are still under development.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Big Tech capex in subsea infrastructure carries tail geopolitical risk; track insurance and rerouting commentary.

insights.claim: A multi-cable disruption during a Taiwan crisis could overwhelm trans-Pacific capacity, with consequences for internet communications, cloud services and financial trading.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Latency and capacity shocks would hit cloud and trading infrastructure; a tail-risk hedge for Asia-exposed digital businesses.
insights.quote: significantly reduce headroom and even overwhelm trans-Pacific capacity as a whole
insights.locator: Paragraphs on single and multiple cable disruption

insights.claim: A CSIS analysis of 200+ research ships from 2020-2025 found China-flagged vessels were outliers in time spent near subsea infrastructure, often performing survey-style tracks near cables rather than mineral-deposit regions.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Persistent mapping is consistent with contingency planning; a leading indicator of gray-zone escalation.

insights.claim: The China-linked vessel Ke Xue made survey-like movements near Russia's government-owned Polar Express cable, suggesting China maps even partner Russia's infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Shows Chinese cable-mapping is not limited to adversaries.
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning "One of the most surprising findings"

insights.claim: A 2025 anchor-dragging incident near Taiwan led to the first Taiwanese conviction of a Chinese captain, sentenced to three years over damage to the Tai-Peng 3 cable.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Legal precedent that raises the cost of deniable cable cutting.

insights.claim: Most cable damage is accidental (bottom trawling, anchors, storms), but rising tensions put suspicious cases under scrutiny as Russian and Chinese 'gray zone' tactics.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Separating accident from sabotage is the attribution problem that governs escalation risk.

insights.claim: The Telegraph found more than 500 incidents of Russian fishing boats loitering near UK-linked cables, and NATO confronted Russian submarines practicing cable disabling near Norway.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: European cable security is an active theme; watch NATO surveillance spending.

insights.claim: Iran has threatened to charge US tech companies fees for cables under the Strait of Hormuz and prepared plans to attack them, after the US and Israel attacked Iran in February 2026.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Middle East cable routes now carry explicit state threats, affecting Gulf data-corridor risk.
